strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates a concrete, previously under-examined failure mode (RoPE phase aliasing under mixed-resolution attention) with a compelling empirical diagnosis (head-wise kappa(delta) curves across timesteps and axes on a real pretrained video DiT).
The proposed fix (CRPA) is simple, principled, and training-free in its core mechanism, directly targeting the diagnosed cause rather than treating symptoms as prior interpolation-based methods do.

Extensive experiments across both image (FLUX) and video (Wan2.1) DiTs, multiple baselines (PI-LR/HR, NTK, PI+NTK, YaRN, RALU, Bottleneck Sampling, ToCa), two- and three-stage schedules, ablations on the boundary module, overhead breakdowns, and compatibility with orthogonal caching-based accelerators (TeaCache, MagCache).

Provides a mathematical decomposition (Eq. 6) that gives intuition for why sharply-tuned multi-frequency phase kernels are sensitive to cross-rate sampling, connecting the empirical observation to a plausible mechanistic explanation.

Good coverage of practical considerations, e.g., quality-cost tradeoff curves, an importance-based saliency-driven region selection use case, and an ultra-high-resolution extension demonstrating scalability of the idea.
Clearly written with helpful toy examples (1D indices) and figures illustrating the index remapping, aiding reproducibility of the core idea.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat inconsistent with the full pipeline: the Boundary Expand-and-Replace module relies on a learned latent up/downsampler (~25M or ~6M parameters) that presumably requires its own training, which is not detailed (training data, procedure, or its dependence on the base model) in the main text.

The theoretical derivation (Eq. 6 and its interpretation) is a content-averaged approximation; the leap from this decomposition to the specific claim that CRPA is the uniquely correct fix is argued informally rather than proven, and no ablation isolates CRPA's benefit from the boundary module's contribution in the main results tables (Tables 1-3) versus the ablation figure only showing qualitative differences.

Baselines are restricted almost entirely to RoPE interpolation variants and a couple of resolution-scheduling methods (RALU, Bottleneck Sampling, ToCa); no comparison to other structural approaches for combining heterogeneous token grids (e.g., learned/trainable positional schemes such as ComRoPE/LieRE mentioned in related work) is provided, despite these being discussed as relevant prior art.

Quantitative gains, while consistent, are sometimes modest relative to the LR+HR reference (e.g., Table 1 total VBench 0.770 vs 0.762 for LR+HR, and technical DOVER scores are close to YaRN in some entries), making it harder to judge how much headroom remains and whether the improvement is practically significant versus statistically/visually significant.

Experiments are limited to two specific base models (Wan2.1-1.3B and FLUX.1-dev); generality of the phase-aliasing diagnosis and CRPA's benefit across other RoPE-based architectures (e.g., different frequency schedules, 3D video RoPE variants, or LLM-adjacent DiTs) is not empirically verified, despite the method being pitched as broadly applicable to 'any pretrained DiT'.

No human preference/user study is included despite generation quality being central to the claims; reliance solely on automated metrics (FID, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, VBench, DOVER) which can be imperfect proxies for perceptual quality, especially for subtle boundary artifacts the paper aims to fix.

The saliency-based region selection pipeline (DeepGazeIIE plus tiny VAE decoding) adds complexity and extra hyperparameters (thresholds, band widths) whose sensitivity is not thoroughly analyzed beyond a single ablation table for npad.

strengths: Provides a clear and well-motivated theoretical and empirical analysis (Sec. 3, Eq. 6, derivation in App. B, κ(Δ) measurements in Fig. 3/15/16/24) that explains why naive RoPE position rescaling fails for mixed-resolution attention in DiTs, identifying the sinusoidal phase-mismatch mechanism as the root cause.

The proposed Phase-Aligned Mixed-Resolution Attention (PMA) is simple, training-free, architecturally non-invasive (only modifies key positions per query-key pair), and incurs negligible overhead (0.3% of total latency per Table 16), which is an attractive practical property.

Extensive and fairly rigorous experimental validation across two modalities (FLUX.1-dev for images, Wan2.1-1.3B/14B for video), multiple RoPE-interpolation baselines (PI-LR/PI-HR, NTK, YaRN, hybrids), and multiple orthogonal acceleration families (samplers, caching, token merging, step-distillation, spatial acceleration methods like RALU/Bottleneck/ToCa), with consistent quality/latency gains.

Good ablations covering the Boundary Expand-and-Replace module, HR-key downsampling strategy, boundary padding size, robustness to different off-the-shelf saliency detectors (including a fixed center-square baseline), and per-component overhead breakdown, which support the design choices.

Demonstrates generality beyond the main two-scale setting: 3- and 4-mixed-resolution generation, integration with ultra-high-resolution extrapolation techniques (CineScale, DyPE) reaching 2K/2048² outputs, and combination with step-distilled models (DMD, FLUX.1-schnell) for additional speedups.

Clear writing, informative figures, an honest limitations section with a documented failure case (Fig. 17), and a reasonably reproducible description of implementation details/hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat inconsistent: while PMA itself requires no training, the accompanying Boundary Expand-and-Replace module relies on a trained latent up/downsampler (25M/6M parameters, trained on Pexels/Aesthetic-Train-V2), so the full pipeline used in most experiments is not purely training-free; this nuance could be stated more prominently in the main text.

Baselines emphasized in the main quantitative tables (PI-LR/PI-HR, NTK, YaRN) are generic RoPE interpolation schemes not specifically designed for mixed-resolution generation; the most directly comparable prior work (RALU) is only compared qualitatively/at the acceleration-comparison level rather than integrated into the core Tables 1–2 mixed-resolution comparison, making it harder to judge the marginal contribution over the closest competitor.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (DOVER, VBench, ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, CLIP score) without any human/user study, which is a notable gap given the paper's central claims about visual fidelity and artifact reduction that are often best judged perceptually.

The saliency-guided region-selection use case, while shown to be robust to detector choice, is a fairly simple heuristic (off-the-shelf saliency models or fixed center masks); no analysis of failure modes when saliency prediction misallocates the HR budget in more complex/cluttered scenes beyond the single failure-case figure.

Experiments are restricted to two moderately sized backbones (FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-1.3B, with only limited qualitative results on Wan2.1-14B); it remains unclear how well the phase-alignment analysis and fix transfer to substantially larger or architecturally different DiTs (e.g., different RoPE parameterizations, non-axis-separable schemes).
